fit_reason: Vertiv makes thermal control systems for data centers, spanning air cooling such as Liebert precision units and chillers and liquid cooling such as coolant distribution units and rack-level heat removal, so it is both an air cooling and a liquid cooling company. Cooling demand grows as data centers are finished and accelerators get denser, and Vertiv sells into both the facility-wide air side and the chip-level liquid side that grows fastest with density. Data center power and thermal infrastructure is the core of its business, and it is one of the largest dedicated data center cooling suppliers.

Trane Technologies makes chillers, air handlers and other HVAC equipment and lists data center HVAC and thermal systems among its offerings, making it an air cooling company with a growing role in heat rejection for liquid-cooled sites. Air cooling grows with every new data center and liquid cooling still needs chillers and heat rejection to carry heat out of the building, so it gains from both parts of the shift. Commercial HVAC is central to its business, and it is one of the largest chiller makers serving data centers.

Johnson Controls designs, makes and services HVAC, chillers, refrigeration and building controls and names data centers among its customers, making it an air cooling company that also supplies heat rejection for liquid-cooled sites. Air cooling grows with each new data center and liquid systems still need chillers to reject heat, so it benefits as sites are finished and as density rises. HVAC and building systems are central to the company, and it is one of the largest commercial chiller suppliers to data centers.

Modine makes precision air conditioning for data centers along with chillers, air handlers, fan walls, coolers and condensers, making it an air cooling company with heat rejection products that also serve liquid-cooled sites. Cooling demand grows as data centers are finished and racks get denser, and Modine's data center line sits directly in that path. Thermal management is the whole business and data center cooling has become its main growth driver, so it is a focused mid-size player in the sub-sector.

AAON makes HVAC equipment including specialized data center cooling, chillers and air handling units, and through its BasX division supplies data center cooling systems, making it an air cooling company with a growing liquid cooling offering. Air cooling grows with every data center and liquid cooling grows as accelerators get denser, so it gains from both. HVAC is its entire business and data centers are a fast-growing share of it, though it is smaller than the largest HVAC makers.

Schneider Electric offers data center solutions that include critical power and cooling, covering air cooling units and liquid cooling, so it is both an air cooling and a liquid cooling supplier. Cooling demand grows as data centers are finished and accelerators get denser, and Schneider sells complete power and cooling packages into those builds. Cooling is a meaningful but smaller part of a company dominated by electrical distribution and automation, though it is a major global supplier to data centers.

nVent makes enclosures, cabinets and physical infrastructure that house server and network equipment and sells through data center installers, which places it in the racks and cooling hardware of liquid cooling. Liquid cooling grows as accelerators get denser and takes racks and liquid distribution hardware fitted to the chips, which is where nVent's data center products sit. Data center cooling is a meaningful part of a broader electrical connection and protection business, and it is an established supplier of enclosures to data centers.

SPX Technologies makes cooling and air movement products through its HVAC segment, including Marley cooling towers and fluid coolers, making it a heat rejection company within the cooling chain. Heat rejection carries heat out of the building for both liquid-cooled and air-cooled sites, so it grows with each new data center and with rising density. HVAC is SPX's largest segment, and Marley is a leading cooling tower brand, though data centers are one end market among several.

Dover makes brazed plate heat exchangers and refrigeration systems in its Climate and Sustainability segment and fluid connection systems in Pumps and Process Solutions, which places it in liquid cooling as a supplier of heat exchange and coolant connection components. Liquid cooling grows as accelerators get denser, and each liquid loop needs connectors and heat exchangers to move coolant and reject heat. These products are a meaningful part of a diversified industrial company, and Dover is a component supplier rather than a system integrator.

Carrier makes commercial and residential HVAC equipment, chillers and refrigeration, making it an air cooling company that also supplies chillers for heat rejection. Air cooling is still needed for the rest of each facility and chillers reject heat from liquid loops, so it gains from new data centers. Commercial HVAC is a meaningful part of a business weighted toward residential HVAC and refrigeration, and Carrier is a major global HVAC maker with a smaller data center position than Trane or Johnson Controls.

Super Micro Computer sells liquid-cooled and air-cooled AI servers and full-rack deployments for AI data centers, which places it in liquid cooling through racks and cold plates built around the accelerators. Liquid cooling grows as accelerators get denser and is installed when a rack is finished, so Supermicro's direct liquid-cooled racks follow accelerator volume. Cooling is a feature of its server and rack business rather than a separate product line, and it is a large supplier of liquid-cooled AI racks.

Legence designs, fabricates and installs HVAC, process piping and other mechanical systems and names data centers first among its markets, which makes it an installer of the air and liquid cooling systems in data centers. Cooling is installed when a site or rack is finished, so mechanical engineering and installation volume rises with data center construction. Building mechanical systems are its core business and data centers are a meaningful share, but it installs rather than makes the cooling equipment.

EMCOR provides mechanical construction including HVAC, refrigeration, central plant heating and cooling and high-purity piping, which makes it an installer of the air and liquid cooling systems in data centers. Lennox makes HVAC and refrigeration equipment, including condensing units and industrial chillers whose uses include cooling in data centers, making it an air cooling company with a small data center line. Air cooling grows with every new data center, but Lennox is concentrated in residential and light commercial heating and cooling. Data center cooling is a minor part of its business and it is a small player in the sub-sector.

Chemours makes refrigerants and thermal management solutions under the Freon and Opteon brands, which supply the fluids used in chillers and in two-phase liquid cooling. Air and liquid cooling both rely on refrigerants and coolants, so fluid demand rises as cooling systems are installed, but the sub-sector values the equipment and systems more than the fluids. Thermal and specialized solutions are one of three segments, and data center cooling is a small part of the company.

Solstice Advanced Materials makes specialty materials including refrigerants and materials used in data center cooling systems, which makes it a supplier of fluids to air and liquid cooling. Cooling systems need refrigerants and coolants, so demand rises as data centers are built, but the sub-sector values the equipment and systems more than the inputs. Data center cooling is one of several end markets and the description is too thin to size it.

Regal Rexnord makes motors, fans and blowers for air handling systems, which supply the air movement inside air cooling equipment. Air cooling grows with every new data center, and air handlers need fans and motors, but its Climate Solutions products serve mainly residential and light commercial systems. Air movement is a meaningful part of a broad industrial powertrain business, and it is a component supplier rather than a cooling system maker.

Ferguson distributes HVAC equipment and pipe, valves and fittings to residential and non-residential contractors and offers fabrication and pre-assembly, which places it as a distributor into the air and liquid cooling systems of data centers. Cooling is installed when a site is finished and both air systems and liquid loops need pipe and valves, so distributors gain from data center construction. Data center cooling is a small part of a broad plumbing and HVAC distribution business, and Ferguson is a distributor rather than an equipment maker.
